flags: Likely overlaps with cards outside this batch (records created anyway): leaf (sermo entry-26, folium); seed and stalk (culina entry-121, sēmen, caulis); peel, verb (culina entry-122, dēcorticō, cutem resecāre); apple, pear, honey (culina entry-82; honey also corpus entry-300); breakfast (culina entry-34); vitamin (culina entry-129, which calls this card “the existing vitamin entry”); sand (aedificatio entry-151, ludi entry-180); ice (culina entry-293); spring (culina entry-260, fōns); grass/lawn (domus entry-424, which points to “the grass entry” for grāmen); parasol (vestitus entry-316 has umbella for umbrella, Traupman 399).

Likely overlaps with the other natura batch: berry (entry-204 has bāca / bacca and prefers bāca); kale (entry-418 gives brassica Sabellica, M-O); west wind (entry-502 gives Zephyrus and points to this weather card for Favōnius); stream (my “brook” in also; entry-505 gives rīvulus for brook); plain (entry-505 gives campus as “open, unploughed field”); fig tree and olive tree (entries 210, 211 have fīcus and olīva for the fruit); cornelian cherry tree and blackthorn (entry-204 has cornum and the sloe).

berry: the card leads with bacca, so it is recommended; but Lewis & Short heads bāca (“less correctly bacca”), the series spelling is bāca (latinitas AGENTS.md §2), the dog-rose quotation from Libellus VII has bācae, and entry-204 prefers bāca. The card’s “equally ancient (L&S)” overstates L&S.

pepō: entry-192 writes pepō, peponis (L&S pĕpo, -ŏnis; Greek -ονος; the decision in notes/food-vocabulary-bulgaria-and-fabulae.md), but entry-110 prints pepō, pepōnis (now the alternative in pumpkin) and entry-191 pepōnēs (onion comment, Vulg. Num. 11, 5). Copied as printed; probably pepon- both times.
mēlo, mēlōnis m. (melon): the nominative is printed without the macron that pepō and mēlopepō have on the same card; L&S prints mēlo, -ōnis, never marking the final o. Copied as printed.
hornbeam: the card writes carpinus, carpinī; Lewis & Short prints carpīnus (long i). No note explains the difference.

Missing macrons in composed examples, copied as printed: “Unum caulem apiī cape.” (celery) and “Unum cochlear sēminis līnī trītī adde.” (flaxseed) want Ūnum (L&S ūnus); “Dimidium avacātum adde.” (avocado) wants Dīmidium (L&S dīmidium).
banana: the Pliny quotation on the card reads arienae, without the ē of the headword ariēna, ariēnae.
peel: the card says Lewis & Short gives no perfect or supine for dēglūbō; L&S has “dē-glūbo, no perf., ptum” (supine dēgluptum). Comment kept as written.
carrot: the card calls carōta “a Late Latin name”; L&S cites only Apicius (3, 21), which converting.md counts as post-classical, so the period is post-classical.
maize: frūmentum Indicum is set renaissance from M-O s.v. corn (1571 Mattioli); the card says only “an attested descriptive alternative”.
celery: helēoselīnum is Traupman’s word on the card; its period is classical because L&S glosses it “smallage, celery” from Pliny.

Periods where the card is silent, set to the later choice: bēta rubra and capsicum rubrum ours; vītamīnicus ours (“not claimed here to be corpus-verified”); rosa canīna modern (Linnaeus’s species name; L&S has no rosa canina; the Libellus VII gloss marks it as a species with Anglicē); arbor citrea modern in the lemon sense (citron tree in L&S).
apple tree: “Spectā mē, Baba! Quam longē saluī!” illustrates no word of the fruit-trees card; it is kept on the card’s main record, as part of the Libellus VII apple-tree scene.

walnut is one record for the nut and the tree (L&S “a walnut; a walnut-tree”; entry-201 lists jūglāns as walnut tree); the other fruit trees, with Latin words of their own (mālus/mālum, pirus/pirum, cerasus/cerasum), are records apart. caulis is in two records: stalk (entry-107, “stalk or stem”) and kale (entry-191, “cabbage stalk, kale”).
herba (“grass, herb”) is only in grass; no herb record was made, since culinary herbs belong with natura entry-212 and culina entry-408.

The cards 105–114 were found by searching “smoothie”; the records do not carry that word, which is not a synonym of any of their senses. Add it to also (or a collection) if that search should keep working.
fog: the evidence “Traupman XV” is Traupman’s chapter XV, The Weather (pp. 132–137), not a page.
Cards 190–192 cite the readers in the older style (Ep. III, Epp. VI–VII, Culīna); kept as written in comments and source lines.

Where the card gave no source of its own for a word, the record carries the card’s readers line (the word occurs in the readers): trunk, bark, elm, pine, pine (adjective), flower, ocean, sand, bank, spring, cistern, west wind, cloud, wind, downhill. poplar has a line of mine stating what L&S has; lemon tree carries the L&S citreum link from entry-114.
Domain: breakfast and recipe are meal and kitchen words (culina); kept in natura, the card’s category.

terms.comment: A modern lexical form. Plural vītamīna, vītamīnōrum n. pl., vitamins, using the neuter form. The international term was coined from “vita” and “amine”; it does not imply that all vitamins are amines. The ī in vīta and the adopted international -amīn- reading give our convention vītamīnum; these are reconstructed Neo-Latin reading quantities, not attested Classical measurements.
The feminine variant, also recorded by Morgan–Owens, without documented stem quantities.
